concept.name: Open interest change
concept.definition: The day-over-day (or period-over-period) change in open interest — the total number of futures contracts, long or short, in a delivery month or market that have been entered into and not yet liquidated by an offsetting transaction or fulfilled by delivery. Rising open interest indicates new positions being created; falling open interest indicates positions being closed.
concept.intuition: Volume counts how many contracts changed hands; the change in open interest tells you whether hands are entering or leaving the market.
concept.mechanics: Computed as OI_t - OI_{t-1} from exchange-published open interest. A trade between two new entrants increases OI by one; between two existing holders closing out, it decreases OI by one; between an entrant and an exiter, OI is unchanged. Analysts combine the sign of the OI change with price direction to infer whether money is flowing into or out of a move.
concept.formula: ΔOI = OI_t - OI_{t-1}, where OI = total open contracts (each counted once, either on the long or short side).
concept.failure_modes: OI changes say nothing about who is trading or their intent — the same increase can be new speculative longs or new commercial shorts. Around contract roll periods, front-month OI mechanically falls while deferred OI rises, so contract-level changes mislead unless aggregated across the curve.
concept.misconceptions: Rising open interest does not mean 'more buyers than sellers' — every futures contract has both a buyer and a seller by construction. It also does not measure volume; high volume with flat OI indicates churn (day trading) rather than new positioning.
concept.example: Crude oil OI rises from 1.80 million to 1.85 million contracts (+50,000) while price rallies $2: new money is entering long and short, which analysts read as fresh positioning behind the move rather than short covering.

citations.source: CFTC Futures Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
